label: M9 S1 | The Universal Ratio Template

formulas.name: The Universal Ratio Formula

variables.meaning: What the business produced — profit, cash flow, revenue, etc.
What the business used to produce it — capital, assets, equity, revenue base, etc.

formulas.worked_example: Take Asian Paints FY23. Revenue = ₹34,488 Cr. Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr. Total Capital Employed = ₹15,200 Cr. Three ratios, three different stories. Net Margin = 4,106 / 34,488 = 11.9% (every ₹100 of sales yields ₹11.9 of profit). ROCE = (Operating Profit ₹5,500 Cr) / 15,200 = 36.2% (every ₹100 of capital yields ₹36 of operating profit). Asset Turnover = 34,488 / (Total Assets ₹19,000 Cr) = 1.81x (each rupee of assets generates ₹1.81 of revenue). Same company. Three lenses. Three insights. Notice how the 11.9% margin alone tells you nothing — 11.9% is low for software (Infosys runs 25%+) but exceptional for paints. That is why lenses must be interpreted in context.
formulas.sensitivity_note: If the output metric grows faster than the input metric, the ratio improves — that is the signature of a scaling business. If input grows faster than output, the ratio deteriorates — the signature of value destruction.

formulas.name: The Time-Series Delta
formulas.worked_example: TCS ROCE moved from 52% in FY22 to 58% in FY23. YoY change = (58 - 52) / 52 × 100 = +11.5%. A double-digit improvement in an already elite ROCE is a massive signal. Always compute the delta — direction matters as much as the level.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A stable ratio in an industry where peers are declining is actually an improvement. Always benchmark the delta, not just the absolute level.

formulas.name: The Universal Ratio Formula

variables.meaning: What the business produced — profit, cash flow, revenue, etc.
What the business used to produce it — capital, assets, equity, revenue base, etc.

formulas.plain_english: A ratio distils any business relationship into a single number by dividing what a company achieved by what it spent to achieve it. This template applies universally: whether measuring profitability (profit ÷ revenue), efficiency (revenue ÷ assets), or return (operating profit ÷ capital), the same structure reveals how effectively a business converts inputs into outputs. Ratios are meaningless in isolation — they only tell a story when compared across time, against peers, or against the company's cost of capital.

worked_example.problem: Analyse Asian Paints' FY23 operating efficiency and capital productivity using the universal ratio template.
steps: Revenue = ₹34,488 Cr; Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr; Operating Profit = ₹5,500 Cr; Total Assets = ₹19,000 Cr; Capital Employed = ₹15,200 Cr.
Net Margin = Net Profit / Revenue = ₹4,106 Cr / ₹34,488 Cr = 0.119 = 11.9%. Interpretation: every ₹100 of sales yields ₹11.9 of net profit.
ROCE = Operating Profit / Capital Employed = ₹5,500 Cr / ₹15,200 Cr = 0.362 = 36.2%. Interpretation: every ₹100 of capital generates ₹36.2 of operating profit.
Asset Turnover = Revenue / Total Assets = ₹34,488 Cr / ₹19,000 Cr = 1.81x. Interpretation: each rupee of assets generates ₹1.81 of annual revenue.

Contextualise: 11.9% margin is low for software (Infosys runs 25%+) but exceptional for paints (commoditised, capital-intense). 36.2% ROCE is elite. Asset turnover of 1.81x suggests efficient asset deployment for a manufacturing company.
worked_example.result: Three ratios, three lenses: Asian Paints is a capital-efficient, high-return business with narrow but respectable margins — typical of a well-run speciality chemical/paint maker.
worked_example.insight: The same company, same year, three different stories. No single ratio answers 'is this business good?' The universal template forces you to ask: good at what? This discipline prevents misinterpretation.

formulas.sensitivity_note: If the output metric grows faster than the input metric, the ratio improves — that is the signature of a scaling business. If input grows faster than output, the ratio deteriorates — the signature of value destruction.

formulas.name: The Time-Series Delta
formulas.plain_english: Tracking how a ratio changes over time reveals momentum and inflection points. A ratio can be good in absolute terms but deteriorating in trend, or vice versa. Computing the year-on-year percentage change normalises the comparison and allows you to distinguish between modest improvements in weak businesses and meaningful declines in strong ones. This delta is your first alarm bell.
computation: Calculate the ratio for the current period.
Calculate the same ratio for the prior period.
Divide the difference by the prior ratio.
Multiply by 100 to express as a percentage.

worked_example.problem: Assess the trend in TCS ROCE between FY22 and FY23.
steps: Interpretation: ROCE improved by 11.5% year-on-year, from an already elite level, indicating accelerating capital productivity.
worked_example.insight: A double-digit improvement in an already elite ROCE (52% is already exceptional) signals very strong momentum. This is not a struggling business inching towards profitability — it is an elite business getting more elite. Always compute the delta; direction matters as much as the absolute level. A stable ROCE at 40% in an industry where peers are declining from 45% to 35% is actually an improvement in competitive position.

formulas.sensitivity_note: A stable ratio in an industry where peers are declining is actually an improvement. Always benchmark the delta, not just the absolute level.
